world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Tharu seems to fall into this latter category, and the following data and analysis are very preliminary, with the following general trends noted: In two and three syllable words, stress tends to be on the penultimate syllable as in: [ˈpu.tʃʰi] 'tail' ... [bə.ˈkʰɑ.ɾi] 'grain bin'. In other cases, however, stress does not seem to be predictable. For example, stress occurs on the last syllable in words that have a closed final syllable as in: [əˈkɑs] 'sky' ... However, there are many exceptions to the above as in: [ˈʈə.nɪk] 'a little bit' ... [ˈso.mɑɾ] 'Monday'. In light of the above, we might make a general statement that stress occurs on the penultimate syllable, but is lexically marked for those words where it occurs on the final syllable.
new_statements.citation: Boehm, Edward D. 2003. A Descriptive Phonology of Dangaura Tharu. Ms. dated February 6, 2003; SIL Language & Culture Archives (https://www.sil.org/system/files/reapdata/15/64/99/156499018526959579362232351120477629534/). 104 pp.
new_statements.locator: Sec. 4.3.1 'Stress system', pp. 49-50 (PDF pp. 60-61); ToC lists 4.3 Stress at p. 49
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of two- and three-syllable words; a subset of words with a closed final syllable take final stress, which the author treats as lexically marked rather than rule-governed (since many closed-final words still have penultimate stress). The author flags the analysis as very preliminary and in need of checking.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress (ˌ) is defined in the symbol list (p. iii) and marked on a number of word-list items (e.g. [ˌpən.ˈbʰəɾ.ni] 'water carrier', [ˈɖu.pə.ˌhəɾ] 'noon', [ˌə.nu.ˈsɑɾ] 'according to'), but no rule for it is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress in some words with a closed final syllable ([əˈkɑs] 'sky', [pi.ˈʈʰɑɾ] 'back', [u.ˈkʰəʈ] 'shallow', [su.ˈkʰɾun] 'drying grain'), against 'many exceptions' with closed final syllable and penultimate stress ([ˈʈə.nɪk], [ˈmu.ɾuʈ], [ˈke.wɒɾ], [ˈkə.ʈjæk], [ˈso.mɑɾ]); the author concludes final stress is lexically marked. Sec. 4.3.2 says the whole area needs further investigation, including the role of vowels.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, isolated word-list items (transcriptions checked with a native speaker, including syllable breaks and stress placement, per the acknowledgements); the author also cites Masica 1991 on Indo-Aryan stress being syllable/mora-timed with complicated rules. Author's own assessment: 'very preliminary'.
new_statements.identity_note: Boehm 2003 describes the Dangaura Tharu of Dang district (Nepal), the variety Glottolog labels dang1260 [thl]; data from named Dangaura Tharu speakers (Kophi Ram Chaudhary, Ashok Tharu). Paudyal's 2013 TU PhD 'A Grammar of Chitoniya Tharu' concerns Chitwania Tharu (chit1274), not this language.

sources.note: Sec. 4.3 'Stress' (pp. 49-50): in 2- and 3-syllable words stress 'tends to be on the penultimate syllable'; in some words with a closed final syllable it falls on the final syllable, with 'many exceptions'; general statement: penultimate stress, lexically marked final stress; data called 'very preliminary'. Secondary stress (ˌ) is marked in the word list but not discussed.
States 34 consonants, 6 vowels, 'non-tonal'; nothing on stress; cites Paudyal 2022 and SIL sociolinguistic surveys.
